title: The Science of Sleep Cycles: Why 90 Minutes Matters

slides.heading: The Science of Sleep Cycles
slides.body: Why 90 minutes is the magic number for waking up refreshed

slides.heading: Sleep Is Not One State
slides.body: While you sleep, your brain cycles through distinct stages — not a single continuous rest. Each cycle moves through light sleep, deep sleep, and REM sleep in a predictable pattern.

slides.heading: The 90-Minute Cycle
slides.body: One complete sleep cycle lasts approximately 90 minutes. A typical night contains 4 to 6 of these cycles. Waking mid-cycle is what causes that groggy, disoriented feeling called sleep inertia.

slides.heading: Stage 1 & 2: Light Sleep
slides.body: The cycle begins with light sleep — your body temperature drops, heart rate slows, and muscles relax. Brain waves slow from the active beta waves of wakefulness down to theta waves. You can be easily woken here.

slides.heading: Stage 3: Deep Sleep (Slow-Wave)
slides.body: Deep sleep is when physical restoration happens. Growth hormone is released, immune function is boosted, and memories are consolidated. Delta brain waves dominate. This stage is hardest to wake from.

slides.heading: REM: The Dream Stage
slides.body: REM (Rapid Eye Movement) sleep is where vivid dreaming occurs. The brain is nearly as active as when awake, but the body is temporarily paralyzed. REM is critical for emotional processing and creative problem-solving.

slides.heading: How Cycles Shift Through the Night
slides.body: Early in the night, cycles contain more deep sleep. As morning approaches, cycles shift heavily toward REM sleep. This is why cutting sleep short robs you disproportionately of REM — your most mentally restorative stage.

slides.heading: Calculating Your Ideal Bedtime
slides.body: Work backwards from your wake time in 90-minute increments, adding 15 minutes to fall asleep. To wake at 6:30 AM: subtract 7.5 hrs (5 cycles) → bedtime is 11:00 PM. Apps like Sleep Cycle use motion sensors to wake you at cycle end.

slides.heading: The Power Nap Science
slides.body: A 20-minute nap keeps you in light sleep and boosts alertness. A 90-minute nap completes a full cycle, improving memory and creativity. Avoid 30–60 minute naps — you'll wake from deep sleep feeling worse than before.

slides.heading: Sleep Smarter, Not Longer
slides.body: Quality sleep is about cycles, not just hours. Align your schedule to 90-minute intervals, protect your REM-rich morning sleep, and your body will do the rest.
